In patients with advanced dilated and ischemic cardiomyopathy and severe functional mitral regurgitation, mitral valve replacement (MVR) may not be the most ideal option. While MVR can provide a temporary solution to alleviate symptoms, it is associated with higher in-hospital and late mortality compared to mechanical valve replacement (MVRR). However, there are situations where MVR might still be preferred.

For instance, if the patient has severe functional MR who has had multiple reoperations due to progressive disease or poor left ventricular function, MVRR might be a better option. Additionally, in some cases, patients with advanced cardiomyopathy may benefit from MVRR as it can provide a more durable solution compared to MVR.

However, for younger patients with dilated and ischemic cardiomyopathy who are asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic, MVR is often considered the preferred approach due to its potential to improve survival and quality of life. The benefits of MVR in this population may be outweighed by the risks, especially considering the high incidence of surgical complications in elderly patients.

It's essential for clinicians to weigh the individual patient factors, including comorbidities, functional status, and personal preferences, before making a decision about mitral valve replacement. A multidisciplinary approach involving cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, and other specialists may be necessary to determine the best course of treatment for each patient.

Ultimately, while MVR can be an effective solution for severe functional MR in patients with advanced dilated and ischemic cardiomyopathy, it is not always the same as MVRR. Careful consideration of individual patient factors and a comprehensive clinical evaluation are crucial to ensure that the most suitable option is chosen.
